Two concepts that keep the system portable

The accessibility tree tells the agent what Windows believes is on screen. The common contract lets every model and every control driver speak the same language.

Accessibility tree

A structured map of controls, names, values, states, positions, and supported actions. Instead of guessing that a blue rectangle is a button, the agent can read “Play button, enabled” and invoke it directly.

Window "Spotify"
├─ Navigation
│  ├─ Button "Home"
│  └─ Button "Search"
└─ Player controls
   ├─ Button "Play" [enabled]
   ├─ Slider "Volume" [64%]
   └─ Text "Current track"

Common contract

A provider-neutral schema for observations, actions, and results. It is not the memory itself. The durable context stays locally; the contract is how selected context and capabilities move between components.

CUA, UIA, Playwright, native Windows

What is a CUA Driver?

CUA means computer-using agent. A driver is the local execution layer—not the intelligence. It collects evidence from the desktop, translates approved actions into Windows behavior, and returns a fresh observation for verification.

1

Perception

Captures displays or windows, enumerates apps, reads accessibility controls, and returns geometry and stable references.

2

Action

Uses semantic UI Automation first, then background messages where possible, and explicit foreground mouse or keyboard input when necessary.

3

Lifecycle

Binds actions to observations, rejects stale targets, supports cancellation, and reports structured failures rather than pretending success.

4

Model boundary

Exposes the same desktop operations through SDK or MCP, so the reasoning model can change without replacing Windows integration.

Why Cua Driver is interestingIts MIT-licensed core already implements much of the ugly Windows machinery and OpenClaw uses its SDK for experimental Windows computer control. But releases are still prerelease-quality, and the optional perception package carries separate AGPL obligations, so it must pass a focused local spike before adoption.

Five approaches, three serious contenders

No single interface wins everywhere. The important architectural choice is whether Hey Computer routes intelligently or bets the entire product on one surface.

ApproachStrengthWeaknessRecommended role
Cua DriverBroad desktop perception and action already builtWindows path is still experimentalFirst general driver
Windows UIA + native APIsFast, structured, low-cost, natural fit for .NETLarge bespoke build; incomplete on custom UIsPreferred native path and fallback
Screenshot + pixel controlWorks anywhere a human can seeSlower, costlier, coordinate-sensitiveUniversal last resort
Playwright / browser structureReliable, fast, easy verification on the webCannot control arbitrary Windows appsBrowser accelerator
App-specific commandsVery fast and deterministicDoes not scale; constant maintenanceOptional learned or curated shortcuts
Practical winner: hybrid routingTry direct APIs or stable app skills, then browser structure, then Windows UIA, then local visual parsing, and finally raw screenshots with foreground mouse and keyboard. Always re-observe and verify.

What is state of the art now?

The leading systems are moving beyond pure visual clicking. They combine perception sources, specialize agents, verify trajectories, and increasingly create or evolve better tool interfaces from experience.

Agent S4

A meta-agent evolves small tool libraries from task experience. Its authors report 21.3% on strict OSWorld V2 with an open model—3.8× the same model with fixed interfaces. The lesson: general control plus evolving shortcuts can outperform a frozen toolset.

Microsoft UFO²

A HostAgent selects applications while AppAgents combine screenshots, UI Automation, native APIs, and knowledge. This is the closest technical precedent for Windows-native, multi-agent hybrid control.

OpenAI and Anthropic

Their APIs define screenshot, mouse, keyboard, and browser tool loops, but the client still owns the actual environment, permissions, session, and cleanup. They are model adapters—not a complete local Windows platform.

OmniParser

Turns screenshots into labeled interactable regions when accessibility data is absent. Useful for custom UIs, but it adds model weight, latency, and licensing considerations.

Published scores use different OSWorld versions, step budgets, and harnesses; they show direction, not a clean leaderboard. Hey Computer needs its own repeatable Windows task suite.

Hey Computer versus OpenClaw

OpenClaw is the closest broad product analogue. It is far ahead in execution infrastructure; our differentiation has to come from a narrower and more coherent personal-computer experience.

DimensionOpenClawHey Computer
Core identityCross-platform gateway for channels, tools, plugins, and remote nodesWindows-native, voice-first personal computer companion
ConversationMessaging and control interfacesAlways-available spoken personality that remains responsive during work
MemoryPersistent workspaces and agent stateInspectable local vault with user-owned continuity and provenance
DelegationAgent runtime, skills, tools, and nodesVisible Conversation → Orchestration + Context → Worker hierarchy
Computer controlNormalized computer tool; experimental Windows plugin embeds pinned CUA SDKReplaceable driver architecture proposed; general control not built yet
Current advantageMaturity, permissions, pairing, plugins, remote execution, lifecycleFocused voice presence, transparent memory, model independence, visible work and budgets
Borrow, do not cloneAdopt OpenClaw’s stable model-facing computer tool, hidden driver boundary, pinned runtime, execution-scoped references, explicit opt-in, and hard cleanup. Preserve Hey Computer’s voice, local context vault, agent tree, and usage governance as the product.

Build the user-owned layer above every model.

Start with Cua Driver behind our own interface. Route browsers through Playwright, native apps through UIA, and use visual mouse-and-keyboard control as the fallback. Keep personality, memory, permissions, task state, audit history, and computer capability local and provider-independent.

First engineering proof

1

Driver spike

Enumerate windows; capture a window and full desktop; read UIA; click, type, scroll, hotkey, and cancel.

2

Contract

Define provider-neutral observations, actions, results, frame identifiers, provenance, and verification evidence.

3

Real test

Complete a task across Settings, a WPF app, and Chrome without app-specific code, while showing every action and allowing immediate stop.
